VASCULAR EMERGENCIES 
 
  
HIGH INDEX OF SUSPICION IS KEY! 
 
ALL VASCULAR EMERGENCIES ARE EXTREMELY TIME 
SENSITIVE – DO NOT DELAY! 
ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM (AAA) 
• History: Sudden onset abdo/flank/back/groin/sciatic pain. Syncope. Hypovolaemic 
shock/Haemodynamic instability if leaking/ruptured. Lower limb ischaemia/cyanosis 
• Physical: Pulsatile abdominal mass (50% of cases). Unexplained hypotension/tachycardia. 
Tender/distended abdomen. May present with melena/GI bleed signs. Abdominal wall 
ecchymosis – flank/umbilical/thigh/scrotum – low sensitivity 
• Risk factors: Male, age >50, smoking, atherosclerosis, hypertension, family history 
• Imaging: POCUS 1st line – OUTER LUMEN TO OUTER LUMEN aorta >3cm diameter = aneurysmal, 
>6cm = high risk of rupture, free fluid = rupture until proven otherwise.  
CTA gold standard – preferred pre-op for surgical planning.  
• UNSTABLE PATIENTS NEED THEATRE, NOT CT! 
• Types: Majority infrarenal, may extend to iliac vessels and beyond 
• Complications: Sudden death. Organ ischaemia – renal, mesenteric, lower limb artery 
involvement. Distal embolization, rhabdomyolysis. 
• Management: Urgent vascular consult!  
Resus as for major trauma – 2 IV lines, consider CVP. Minimise clear IV fluids. Crossmatch for 
massive transfusion, emergency blood in interim. Hypotensive resuscitation – aim for systolic BP 
80 – 90 mmHg. Tranexamic Acid 1g stat, Fentanyl 1µg/kg analgesia. Labetalol infusion (see 
protocol) if HPT emergency. 
	
THORACIC AORTIC ANEURYSM/DISSECTION 
• History: Sudden tearing central chest pain, radiating to back.  Sudden neuro deficit. 
• Physical: May present as HPT emergency, ACS, CVA, ADHF, SVC syndrome, pericardial 
tamponade. Pulse/BP discrepancy, new aortic regurg murmur, unexplained 
syncope/hypotension 
• Risk factors: As for AAA, connective tissue d/o, bicuspid aortic valve, syphilis. 
• Imaging: CXR – widened mediastinum, loss of aortic knuckle, calcium sign. POCUS – widened 
aortic root, pericardial effusion.  CTA gold standard 
• Types: Stanford A: Any ascending aorta involvement. Stanford B: Descending aorta only. 
• Complications: Sudden death, stroke, MI, pericardial tamponade, ADHF due to valvular 
regurgitation. 
• Management: Urgent cardiothoracic consult!  
As for AAA. NB! Pain control. Labetalol infusion 1st – aim for pulse < 60 bpm,  
Systolic BP < 110 mmHg. Add Nitrocine infusion (see protocol) if BP still elevated. 
 
CRITICAL AND ACUTE LIMB ISCHAEMIA 
 
• History: New/worsening pain/claudication, altered 
sensation, muscle weakness. The 6 P’s = LATE SIGN 
• Physical: Cold, blue/mottled limb, decreased/absent 
pulses, tissue necrosis. 
§ Embolus: Acute onset, complete cutoff, no prior 
claudication/skin changes/ ulcers/bruits 
*clinical diagnosis* 
§ Thrombosis: Chronic, usually good collaterals, 
history of claudication/ulcers/chronic skin 
changes/bruits *CTA diagnosis* 
• Risk factors: Smoking, atherosclerosis, hypertension, AF, 
large vessel aneurysms (AAA, fem/pop disease), DVT, 
DM 
• Investigations: Handheld Doppler, ankle brachial index  
(ABI) < 0.5 = SEVERE ARTERIAL ISCHAEMIA, CT Angio 
• Complications: Limb loss, rhabdomyolysis 
• Management: Urgent vascular consult!  
Fluid bolus, maintain systemic BP (MAP > 65mmHg), 
adequate analgesia, O2 if necessary. Anticoagulation in 
consultation with Vascular Surgery team. 
• ABI        =  HIGHEST PRESSURE IN FOOT 
  HIGHEST PRESSURE IN BOTH ARMS 
Dr du Plessis / Dr R Gihwala CMJAH Emergency Department June 2020
